Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette: John is a 66-year-old European-American male who presents with significant symptoms of PTSD stemming from childhood physical abuse by his caregiver. John's current occupation as a software engineer and his marital status are integral to understanding the impact of his trauma on his daily life. John vividly recalls the intense experiences of growing up in an environment where safety was never guaranteed. The memories still surface unexpectedly, often triggered by sudden changes in temperature or the rapid beating of his own heart. These intrusive thoughts transport him back to moments when he felt helpless and vulnerable. For example, a cold breeze might trigger a memory of being physically punished on a chilly winter evening. John's heart racing during intense work deadlines can similarly evoke painful recollections. John has developed extensive avoidance behaviors as a way to cope with these triggers. He meticulously avoids paying attention to his own body, fearing that any bodily sensation could be a harbinger of danger. His aversion extends to social interactions; he has distanced himself from friends and colleagues who knew him before the trauma occurred. This avoidance is not just about staying away from people but also about shielding himself from potentially triggering environments. John's heightened sense of vigilance shapes his daily life significantly. He constantly notices potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, convinced that his body reacts to danger even before he has time to think. A simple touch can startle him severely, as if the threat is ever-present and ready to strike. John believes he must be especially careful because you never know what could happen next. This constant state of alertness makes it difficult for him to relax or trust others. John's mistrust extends beyond his immediate environment; he feels like an outsider in social settings and at work. His colleagues have noticed a marked change in his behavior over the years, from becoming more reclusive to showing signs of anxiety during team meetings. The accumulation of these avoidance behaviors has led to significant relational changes. John finds it challenging to maintain close friendships or engage in meaningful conversations with others, further reinforcing his sense of isolation. John's current state reflects a culmination of years of coping mechanisms that have gradually strained his relationships and impacted his professional life. It was not until recently, when his wife expressed concern about the growing distance between them, that John realized he needed help. He is most afraid of being alone and misunderstood but also hopes for understanding and support to regain some sense of normalcy in his life. John's story illustrates how childhood trauma can cast a long shadow over adult life, shaping one's perceptions and interactions with the world. His journey toward healing involves navigating these deeply ingrained fears and mistrust while finding new ways to connect with others and feel safe again.
